title: What are the landmark numbers of a base three system?
description: Groups of three build up on the board: one, then three of those, then three of those, and so on. Five landmark numbers appear, and fifty is broken into them by taking the biggest that fits each time. Keeko's doubt is that landmarks are found by adding three each time.
teaching_notes: One idea: in a base three system each landmark is three times the one before, so multiply to get the landmarks and then take the biggest that fits. Watch for students who add the base instead of multiplying by it.

source: Find the first five landmark numbers of a base-3 system and write 50 as a sum of them.
video_script.why: The child sees that landmark numbers of a base n system come from multiplying by n, then writes a number as a sum of them.
video_script.substitution: Start at one and multiply by three each time, then take the biggest landmark that fits.
video_script.anchor: a row of groups: one, three of those, three of those again, as the book builds its landmark numbers
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko adds three each time to get landmarks; but three ones make three, three threes make nine, and each landmark is three times the one before
video_script.payoff_line: The landmarks are one, three, nine, twenty seven and eighty one.

final_answer.spoken: the landmarks are one, three, nine, twenty seven and eighty one, and fifty is twenty seven plus nine plus nine plus three plus one plus one

maths_rules: Keeko's slip: 3, 6, 9, 12 adds 3 each time; 6 and 12 are not groups of threes made of the landmark before
video_script.design: One idea: multiply by the base to get landmarks, then biggest first. The row of landmarks stays on the board while the working fills in below it.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; five empty boxes in a row; the number 50 with an empty box

marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.ask: five empty boxes appear and the number 50 with its empty box

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about counting in groups of three.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>We must find the first five landmark numbers of this system. Then we must write fifty as a sum of them.
What are the five landmark numbers?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board with the five empty boxes

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: one dot; three dots grouped into a bundle; three bundles grouped into a bigger bundle

marks.first: a single dot appears as the first landmark
marks.next: three of the group before are bundled into the next group
marks.base: the words base three system appear under the bundles

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Landmark numbers are the group sizes we count with. The first landmark number is always one.
<bookmark mark='next'/>We put three of the group before together, and that makes the next landmark.
<bookmark mark='base'/>A system built this way is called a base three system.

marks.given: base 3 and the number 50 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, a base three system and the number fifty.

beats.on_screen: To find: first five landmarks; 50 as a sum of them

marks.find: the two things to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the first five landmark numbers, and write fifty as a sum of them.

marks.start: 1 is written as the first landmark
marks.mult: each landmark is multiplied by 3 to give the next, 3, 9, 27 and 81

narration: <bookmark mark='start'/>Step one, start at one and multiply by three each time. This is because each landmark is three of the one before.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>One times three is three. Three times three is nine. Nine times three is twenty seven, and twenty seven times three is eighty one.

marks.skip: 81 is crossed out because it is more than 50
marks.fit: one 27 is taken and 50 - 27 = 23 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='skip'/>Step two, take the biggest landmark that fits. Eighty one is more than fifty, so we skip it.
<bookmark mark='fit'/>Twenty seven fits once, because two twenty sevens would be fifty four. Fifty take away twenty seven leaves twenty three.

marks.nines: two 9s and the line 2 x 9 = 18 appear

narration: <bookmark mark='nines'/>Step three, count the nines in twenty three. Two times nine is eighteen, and three nines would be twenty seven, which is too many.
<bookmark mark='left'/>Twenty three take away eighteen leaves five.

marks.ones: two 1s appear for the last two

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step four, count the threes in five. One three fits, because two threes would be six. Five take away three leaves two.
<bookmark mark='ones'/>Each one is worth one, so the last two are two ones.

marks.sum: the sum for 50 is written and boxed

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The landmarks are one, three, nine, twenty seven and eighty one.
<bookmark mark='sum'/>Fifty is twenty seven plus nine plus nine plus three plus one plus one. These parts add back to fifty.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the row of landmarks
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's list 3, 6, 9, 12 beside a bundle of 9 and 3 loose items; the list is crossed out and 1, 3, 9, 27 is written

marks.bundle: a bundle of 9 with 3 loose items shows 12 is not a new group
marks.fix: the list is crossed out and 1, 3, 9, 27 is written

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the landmarks are three, six, nine, twelve, adding three each time.
<bookmark mark='bundle'/>But twelve is only one bundle of nine and three loose items, which is not a new group.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The next group must hold three whole bundles of nine, so we multiply by three and never add.
